extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, researchers, archaeologists, geneticists, museum and conservation professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for designing and reporting experiments that critically test scientific interpretations (distinguishing mere replication of phenomena from decisive hypothesis tests). Includes related standards for archaeological excavation, conservation, and publication as exemplified by the pieces on Mendelian experiments and Egyptian excavations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing the interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "What I mean by 'testing the interpretation' is the carrying out, by one who is actively sceptical of Mendel's hypothesis, of an experiment of such a kind that the result can leave no doubt in the mind of the experimenter as to the validity, or otherwise, of the hypothesis tested."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An experiment to test an interpretation must be designed by a sceptical investigator and be capable of producing a decisive outcome; mere repetition of observations that are consistent with an interpretation does not qualify. The author gives a concrete suggested cross (see related criterion) as an example of such a decisive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish phenomenon from interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Mendelian phenomenon is a fact; but the Mendelian interpretation is an inference, and it is dangerously misleading not to lay stress on the distinction between the two."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating experimental work or reporting results, explicitly separate the observed facts from the interpretive inferences. Avoid treating an interpretation as if it were observational fact; state assumptions and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication is not equivalent to critical testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer objects to the statement that 'no one has repeated Mendel's experiments with the deliberate intention of testing the Mendelian interpretation,' clarifying that many experiments have 'repeated and confirmed' Mendel's results but were not undertaken with the deliberate intention of critically testing the interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish studies that merely reproduce phenomena from studies deliberately designed to discriminate between competing hypotheses. Report authors' intentions and the criticality of design when claiming independent confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design decisive critical experiments (example provided)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested experiment: test whether the 75% yellow / 25% green proportion for F2 from crosses between pure yellow and pure green holds when the green parent is an 'extracted green' from an F1 line with many yellow ancestors (i.e., a green whose parents/grandparents/etc. were yellow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crosses or experimental manipulations that would, under the tested interpretation, produce the same quantitative prediction; if the prediction fails, the interpretation is refuted. The example illustrates designing an experiment that would leave 'no doubt' about the interpretation if results conform or contradict prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of water-damaged funerary woodwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that 'most of the woodwork will not bear handling; much, however, including the skull and bones of the queen, has been preserved by means of boiling paraffin wax, which soaks into the porous substance to which it is applied and solidifies it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle water-damaged wooden funerary objects with extreme care; where appropriate and after assessment, consolidate porous organic materials (e.g., with molten or heated paraffin wax as historically used) to stabilize them. Note: the page describes the practice historically; modern conservators should assess compatibility and long-term effects before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum display ethics for human remains
rubrics_metrics.description: "It seems doubtful whether the actual features of these dead princes should be exposed to the gaze of every vulgar tourist...a more reverent taste will eventually withhold these august bodies from the indignity of public exhibition in glass cases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ethical implications, dignity, and public taste when exhibiting human remains; restrict sensational or gratuitous display and favor restrained, reverent presentation or limited access where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic multi-season archaeological exploration and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of Prof. Naville's ten-season work at Deir el-Bahari involving principal assistants, regular staff, volunteers, plan preparation by designated surveyors, and fragment reconstruction by a specialist (Madame Naville).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archaeological projects should be systematic, often requiring multiple seasons, clearly defined staff roles (directors, assistants, surveyors, volunteers), careful planning, and specialist work (e.g., reconstructing sculpture). Proper organization and continuity across seasons is a quality standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of tomb context via material evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference that re-interment in the King's Valley took place in the reign of Tutankhamon is 'shown by the discovery in the tomb of seals bearing his name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct material markers (seals, inscriptions, stratigraphy, tomb condition) to infer chronology, reburial events, and provenance. Interpretative claims about sequence or date should be tied to concrete archaeological evidence and explicitly reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and communication of excavations for both lay and specialist audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The account contrasts a discovery 'which will appeal to the minds of all, even those entirely ignorant of archaeological science' (the body of Queen Tii) with one 'which will appeal more to the architect and the student of Egyptian religion' (the tomb-shrine of Mentuhetep), and includes photographs and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting excavations, provide material that serves both popular and specialist readerships: narrative/contextual descriptions and broader-interest details for lay readers, plus technical descriptions, plans, photographic documentation, and specialist interpretation for experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial research institute design and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a milling research institute 'containing administrative offices and laboratories, together with an experimental granary, a wheat and rye mill, and a bakery' and objectives 'to carry out practical research and scientific investigation on grain during storing, milling, working up and baking; to experiment with the baking of home and imported grain; to conduct research work for the Government, and to carry out official and private analyses of grain, flour, fodder stuffs, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial research facilities should combine practical experimental plants and laboratories, be capable of handling production-scale samples, and undertake both fundamental and applied investigations for private and public clients. Appropriate funding and institutional partnerships (state + industry) are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: State funding sufficiency as a metric of national scientific support
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary comparison: 'the State grant for the current year towards scientific research in the United States amounts approximately to two and three-quarter millions sterling, that in the United Kingdom... reaches a quarter of a million sterling...the United States attaches seven times as much importance to scientific assistance as the mother country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess national commitment to science by comparing absolute and relative levels of state funding; use such comparisons to argue for policy changes or increased support where appropriate. Reporting should contextualize amounts relative to national revenue and needs.
